name: TypeScript
summary: Typed superset of JavaScript that has become the default for non-trivial frontend code.
what_it_is: A language that adds static types to JavaScript and compiles to plain JavaScript, with type information erased at build time. Its structural type system is designed to describe existing JavaScript patterns rather than impose new ones.
why_it_matters: TypeScript stopped being a choice somewhere around 2020: libraries ship types, editors assume them, and most job postings expect it. The value is less about catching bugs than about editor tooling — accurate autocomplete and safe renames across a large codebase change how quickly you can work in unfamiliar code. If you last evaluated it early and found the tooling immature, that objection has expired.
suitable_for: Any codebase more than one person maintains
Long-lived projects where refactoring safety matters
Library authors, whose consumers now expect type definitions
not_suitable_for: Throwaway scripts and prototypes, where the build step is pure overhead
Teams unwilling to invest in learning the type system, who will reach for `any` and get the cost without the benefit
verifiable_facts: Actively maintained by Microsoft; official documentation is current.
Compiles to JavaScript with types erased at build time.
editorial_interpretation: That it is "effectively expected" on team-maintained applications.
That editor tooling, not bug-catching, is its main payoff.
context_dependent_guidance: Suitable: Any codebase more than one person maintains

evidence_gaps: No measured adoption evidence in this product. The claim that it is a default rests on editorial judgement alone.
wrong_if: A reviewer judges that its cost is understated for teams without type-system experience, or that "expected" overstates what the evidence supports.
